det3 multi-particle events: what the second particles are, choosing the trigger track, and a real two-track benchmark

det3 golden row sat_det3 (6-27 Saturday scan, long run, 490 V), production final_phys forward fits (wft) and the phys bundle; M3 v2 rays and the C22 M3 cluster trees. Geometry is from the waveform fits only, never from hit times. Generated by rerun/multiparticle/make_report.py, 2026-10-26.

Verdict

  1. The second particles are secondary electrons knocked out of the material above det3 by the triggering muon, mostly in or just under the upper M3 doublet. They are in time with the muon (91 % within ±150 ns; an unrelated particle would give ~11 %), they point back to the muon (39 % pass within 20 mm of it, against 10 % for two unrelated muons), and where they do, they meet it at Z = 1050–1302 mm in 25 of 44 events (unrelated muons 12 %). They are far steeper than the muons (median |tan| 0.39 against 0.17), mostly MIP-like in charge with a heavy tail (27 % above 2× the single-track median, singles 9 %), and M3 does not see them along their line (any upper-plane match 18 % vs 13 %–20 % for the nulls; none on all four upper planes). Independent coincident muons are excluded (expected 0.432 events); knock-ons made in det3's own gas do not form a separate cluster (0 vertices in the gap) — they are the δ-blob class.
  2. Yes, there is a reference-free rule that beats production on these events. Among the particle candidates of a view, production's choice is the M3 particle 54 % of the time (chance 50 %). "Most vertical" alone gives 70 %; a 5-feature conditional logit (|tan|, prompt t0, time extent, χ²/dof, telescope acceptance), trained on even events and tested on odd and vice versa, gives 80 %, and 77 % with det3-only features. Events with every view right: 69 → 104 of 187 (+0.54 points of interior efficiency, with the multi-track credit). C22's rules (charge, column, χ², t0) indeed do not beat production; the gain comes from the muon being steeper than its secondaries — a property of the cosmic trigger, not of X17 pairs.
  3. Two-track benchmark (det3, bench overlay with M3 truth on both tracks): both tracks found 0 % below 12 mm, 22 % at 12–18 mm, ≥ 97.5 % from 18 mm (production seeder). Above 24 mm: separation σ 0.73 mm per view, opening angle σ 1.47°, closest-approach σ 8.9 mm, vertex height σ 47 mm (opening > 10°). The second track does not move the first at ≥ 18 mm (shift vs its single fit < 0.01 mm); real events agree (M3 leg at single-track resolution beyond 30 mm, 0.70 mm / 1.28° below). Joint two-track fit: 0–6 mm 28 %, 6–12 mm 42 %, 12–18 mm 50 %, 18–24 mm 98 %; singles split 0 % of 30.

1. What the second particles are

Sample. The 187 multi-particle events of multitrack.py: an interior M3 recipe ray through det3 and ≥ 2 particle-like production candidates (summed signal ≤ 24 samples, so a drift column, not a noise band) in a view. In each view the M3 particle is the candidate nearest the ray at the mesh within 5 mm. In 114 events the M3 particle and one other are found in both views; the other x and other y then make a 3-D line (2×2 is unambiguous once the M3 legs are known). The rest are 1×2 / 2×1 (an overlap in one projection) or have the M3 particle missing.

Frames. Raw strip frame with the M3 ray carried into it; Z is M3's (up; det3 mesh at 715, M3 at 1302/1185 and 144/24 mm). The M3 tangent is d pos / d Z and the wft ladder tangent is calibrated on it, so the lines compose.

The material estimate: 0.5–1 g/cm² of detector and frame in the lower plane of the upper M3 doublet (an assumption: the plane's build is not documented here) gives 4–8 % of muons a knock-on above 1 MeV; with the geometric chance of landing in det3's interior ≥ 20 mm from the muon in both views of order a third, that is 1–3 % per trigger, the order of the observed 1.8 % (2×2) and 2.9 % (all multi-particle). This is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a prediction; a Geant4 run of the bench stack would make it one.

Charge. Median 1.16 of the single-track median per unit path (the muon in the same events 1.10): above ~0.5 MeV an electron is near minimum ionising. The tail (27 % above 2×, singles 9 %) is consistent with lower-energy electrons (dE/dx doubles near ~50–80 keV) or two overlapping secondaries — the histogram shows a second bump near 2.3–2.6×, which is what two minimum-ionising particles sharing one cluster (a photon conversion pair, or two knock-ons) would give. It cannot be split further from these fits.

M3. The M events have extra M3 clusters about twice as often as clean singles on every plane (e.g. upper x 28 % vs 15 %), but not on the second particle's line beyond the nulls. Two readings, not separable here: the secondaries are made below the upper doublet's planes, or above and scattered out of the 20 mm window (an MeV electron scatters ~15° in 0.5 m of air plus det3's window). M3 never reconstructs them as a 4-layer track: 13 of the 187 events have an alternative χ² < 1 combination in some view, and an alternative χ² < 5 combination lies on the second particle (≤ 5 mm, Δtan < 0.1) in one view of 1 event and in both views of 0. So there is no real-data sample with telescope truth on both tracks.

2. A reference-free rule to choose the triggering track

296 views (of the multi-particle events) hold the M3 particle among ≥ 2 particle candidates (597 candidates, chance 50 %). A rule sees only det3 and the fixed telescope geometry ("acc": the candidate's projection stays inside the region recipe rays cross on all four M3 planes — a triggering particle must cross them). The logits are conditional (softmax over a view's candidates), L2-regularised, trained on even event ids and tested on odd and vice versa; weights per fold are in choose.json.

Medians, M3 particle vs other: |tan| 0.10 vs 0.19, χ²/dof 67 vs 96, strips 11.5 vs 14, log charge 0.06 vs 0.15. Event level (all 187 multi-particle events, every view must end on the M3 particle; views where it was not found count as failures): production rank 69, in acceptance then rank 93, most vertical 84, logit noacc 103, logit 5 104, logit all 104. The ceiling is the share of events in which the M3 particle is a candidate in both views: 80 % (150 of 187, multitrack.json "any").

Why this differs from C22. C22's twotrack.py tried production rank, largest charge, longest column, lowest χ² and closest t0 on all outliers; here too none of those beats production (largest charge is worse: 43 %). The working feature is inclination: the trigger telescope accepts near-vertical muons, while their secondaries are steep. It is a property of the cosmic trigger. On n_TOF, where every track counts and no track is "the trigger", there is nothing to choose; for the bench efficiency it moves the multi-particle class.

3. The two-track benchmark

Overlay with truth on both tracks (rerun/satstudy/overlay.py; arms re-run by overlay_arm.py with WFT_DEAD_SEED=0, as the 10-26 run): two clean det3 single tracks whose t0 agree within 30 ns, summed in the waveforms (the second track's footprint ± 5 mm, its noise added there), 40 pairs per separation bin. A track is found when a distinct candidate lies within 2 mm of its own single fit. Truth for the resolutions is each donor's M3 ray.

How it relates to T1 / T2 (SAME_CHAMBER_PAIRS.md)

  • T1 (two-track separation) measured on n_TOF run_145 with the beam seeder: physical limit ~1 strip pitch, real-track limit 2–3 mm with the fixed chain + joint fit; coincident overlay pairs below 12 mm found 19 → 58 % (A), 36 → 49 % (C). The det3 bench with the production (bench) seeder is cut at its 12 mm seed gap: 0 % below 12 mm, ~22 % at 12–18, then fully efficient. The bench is therefore limited by the seeder, not by physics: with the joint two-track fit (production settings, F = 300) both are found in 28 %, 42 %, 50 % of the 0–6 / 6–12 / 12–18 mm pairs with 0 of 30 clean singles split, and the recovered pairs keep ~1 mm separation resolution. That is the same scale as T1's beam overlay (A < 12 mm 58 %, C 49 % with its tuned F). The re-pass on n_TOF lost pairs below ~20 mm in either view — the same scale.
  • T2 (single-track angle truth): at ≥ 18 mm the second track does not perturb the first (fits identical to the singles to < 0.01 mm, 0.05°), so pair angles inherit T2's single-track angle scale and resolution directly; the pair opening-angle resolution is √2 × the single-track angle (≈ 1.4–1.5° on det3).
  • Vertex. σ(Z_v) ≈ σ(sep) / tan(opening): 14 mm × 1/tan(open) here. T1's pair_angle.py: a common-vertex pair diverges by only 0.13 × its separation across the 30 mm gap, so close pairs are parallel inside one chamber; the in-chamber vertex is weak and a vertex needs the second chamber's lever arm.

What this does not rule out

  • The vertex heights are straight-line extrapolations of particles that are mostly MeV electrons; multiple scattering in air and in det3's window smears them by ~0.1 m and biases them low. "Made in or just under the upper M3 doublet" is the best reading, not a measurement of the production point. The material between det3 and the doublet, and the doublet's own build, are not documented here.
  • The δ and air-shower rates are labelled estimates (PDG knock-on formula, rule-of-thumb flux, assumed material thickness); they bound orders of magnitude only. No simulation of the bench stack was run.
  • Charge cannot tell an electron above ~0.5 MeV from a muon; the high-charge tail is not resolved into low-energy electrons vs two overlapping secondaries.
  • The choosing rule is trained on 296 views (2-fold by event parity; paired held-out comparison p ≈ 1e-11 against production, ≈ 0.01 against the parameter-free acceptance rule). Its main lever, inclination, belongs to the cosmic trigger and does not transfer to beam data.
  • The overlay sums two single tracks of different triggers: their ionisation is real, but the pair is unrelated (no common vertex, t0 within 30 ns by selection), and only the second track's footprint ± 5 mm is added. Real two-track events with truth on both legs do not exist here: M3 does not reconstruct the second particle.
  • All of this is det3 at one operating point (490 V, bench gas); the 12 mm seeder gap and the noise are bench settings, and the spark-vetoed events (126, 1.95 %; 45 of them showers) are not in the 187.
